definition: seeming reasonable or likely to be true

examples.text: The team offered a plausible explanation for the sudden drop in the lake's oxygen levels.
Historians consider it plausible that traders carried the disease along the river routes.
Maya needed a plausible excuse for missing practice, so she said her bike had a flat tire.

confused.note: Plausible means believable; feasible means possible to carry out.

questions.passage: When marine biologists first proposed that the tiny shrimp could stun prey with sound alone, many colleagues were skeptical. But after high-speed cameras recorded the snap of the claw and the shock wave it produced, the idea came to seem entirely ______ to even its early critics.
questions.explanation: The cameras supplied evidence, so the once-doubted idea now seems believable.

distractors.why: Dubious means doubtful, the opposite of how the critics came to see the idea.
Arbitrary means based on whim, which does not describe an idea backed by evidence.
Obsolete means out of date; the idea was newly accepted, not outdated.

definition: present or found everywhere

examples.text: Microplastics are now ubiquitous, turning up in ocean trenches, mountain snow, and tap water.
By the 1920s the automobile had become ubiquitous on American city streets.
Phone chargers are so ubiquitous in our house that there is one in every room.

confused.note: Prevalent means common in a place or time; ubiquitous is stronger and means seemingly everywhere.

questions.passage: In the early 1990s, few households owned a device that could connect to the internet. Three decades later, such devices are ______: they sit in pockets, hang on kitchen walls, and are even built into refrigerators and doorbells.
questions.explanation: The examples after the colon show the devices are found everywhere.

distractors.why: Scarce means hard to find, the opposite of the situation described.
Obsolete means no longer in use, but the passage says the devices are in heavy use.
Ephemeral means short-lived; the passage is about how widespread the devices are, not how long they last.

definition: having more than one possible meaning; not clear

examples.text: The novel's ambiguous ending leaves readers arguing about whether the narrator ever returned home.
The treaty's ambiguous wording allowed both nations to claim the same strip of land.
Her text was ambiguous, so I could not tell whether "fine" meant she was happy or annoyed.

confused.note: Ambiguous describes words or situations with unclear meaning; ambivalent describes a person with mixed feelings.

questions.passage: The poem's final line can be read as either a celebration of the speaker's freedom or a lament for her loneliness. Critics have debated this ______ line for decades without settling on a single interpretation.
questions.explanation: The line supports two different readings, which is what ambiguous means.

distractors.why: Explicit means clearly stated, but the line's meaning is still disputed.
Ambivalent describes a person's mixed feelings, not a line of text with two meanings.
Redundant means needlessly repeated, which the passage does not suggest.

definition: doubtful; not to be trusted or relied on

examples.text: The supplement's makers cited a dubious study that had tested only six people.
The general's memoir makes the dubious claim that he opposed the invasion from the start.
I was dubious about the secondhand laptop until I saw it start up in seconds.

confused.note: A claim is dubious; the person who doubts it is skeptical.

questions.passage: The website promised that its app could double a user's reading speed in a single afternoon. Because the company offered no data and refused to name the researchers involved, reviewers regarded the promise as ______ at best.
questions.explanation: With no data and unnamed researchers, the claim cannot be trusted.

distractors.why: Empirical means based on observation or data, which is exactly what the claim lacks.
Modest means limited or humble, but doubling reading speed in one afternoon is a bold claim.
Plausible means believable, the opposite of how reviewers judged the promise.

definition: honest and direct, even about unpleasant things

examples.text: In candid letters to her sister, the poet admitted that fame had made her miserable.
The senator's candid diary reveals doubts he never voiced in public.
I asked my coach for a candid opinion, and she told me my serve needed real work.

confused.note: Candor is the noun; candid is the adjective.

questions.passage: Most chief executives describe a failed product in vague, upbeat language. Lin did the opposite. In a ______ memo to her staff, she listed each of her own mistakes and explained exactly how the launch had gone wrong.
questions.explanation: Listing her own mistakes plainly shows honesty and directness.

distractors.why: Evasive means avoiding a direct answer, which describes the other executives, not Lin.
Cursory means quick and shallow, but the memo was detailed and exact.
Benevolent means kind and generous; the passage stresses honesty, not kindness.

definition: very plain and simple; strict or severe in manner

examples.text: The monks lived in austere stone cells with only a bed, a table, and a candle.
The narrator remembers her grandfather as an austere man who rarely smiled or raised his voice.
After the holidays we kept to an austere budget with no restaurant meals for a month.

confused.note: Austere describes plain style or strict manner in general; ascetic describes a person who gives up comforts on purpose.

questions.passage: Visitors expecting gilded ceilings and velvet curtains are surprised by the concert hall's ______ interior: bare concrete walls, plain wooden benches, and a single row of white lamps.
questions.explanation: Bare walls and plain benches describe a severely simple space.

distractors.why: Ornate means richly decorated, the opposite of bare concrete and plain benches.
Obsolete means outdated; the passage describes plainness, not age.
Eclectic means drawn from many varied styles, but the interior shows one bare style.

definition: no longer used because something newer has replaced it

examples.text: Vacuum tubes became obsolete once transistors could do the same job in a fraction of the space.
The longbow was made obsolete by firearms that needed far less training to use.
My brother keeps an obsolete flip phone in his desk drawer as a souvenir.

confused.note: Obsolete means replaced and no longer used; archaic means very old and old-fashioned, though it may survive in special uses.

questions.passage: For most of the twentieth century, ships found their position with paper charts and radio beacons. Satellite navigation has made those radio beacons largely ______, and many of the towers have since been taken down.
questions.explanation: A newer technology replaced the beacons, and the towers were removed.

distractors.why: Ubiquitous means found everywhere, but the beacons are disappearing.
Ambiguous means unclear in meaning, which does not describe equipment.
Indispensable means absolutely necessary, the opposite of something being taken down.

definition: dealing with problems in a practical way instead of following theory or ideals

examples.text: A pragmatic leader, she traded with rival states whenever it helped feed her people.
The engineers took a pragmatic approach and reused a proven engine design.
Being pragmatic, Dad bought the used minivan that fit our budget over the sports car he loved.

confused.note: A pragmatic person does what works; a dogmatic person insists on fixed beliefs.

questions.passage: The mayor had campaigned on building an entirely new subway line. Once in office, however, she proved ______: with funds limited, she chose to add bus lanes, which cost a fraction as much and could open within a year.
questions.explanation: She set aside an ideal plan for a practical, affordable one.

distractors.why: Dogmatic means rigidly holding to one's beliefs, but she changed her plan to fit the facts.
Apathetic means not caring, yet she still acted to improve transit.
Extravagant means spending too much, the opposite of choosing the cheaper option.

definition: to make a problem or bad situation worse

examples.text: Paving over wetlands can exacerbate flooding because the water has nowhere to drain.
The new tax exacerbated tensions between the colonies and the crown.
Scratching the mosquito bite will only exacerbate the itch.

confused.note: Exacerbate means to make a problem worse; exasperate means to annoy a person.

questions.passage: City planners hoped that widening the highway would ease traffic. Instead, the extra lanes drew thousands of new drivers, and the change seemed only to ______ the congestion it was meant to solve.
questions.explanation: "Instead" signals the opposite of easing: the congestion got worse.

distractors.why: Alleviate means to lessen, which is what planners hoped for, not what happened.
Exasperate means to irritate a person; a traffic problem is made worse, not annoyed.
Refute means to prove a claim false, which does not fit an action done to congestion.

definition: something that is different from what is normal or expected

examples.text: The warm patch of ocean was an anomaly that forecasters could not explain.
A peaceful transfer of power was an anomaly in that century of coups.
A snow day in April is an anomaly in our town.

confused.note: Both mean a departure from normal; aberration often suggests the departure is unwelcome.

questions.passage: Every other sensor on the bridge reported steady readings throughout the night. One gauge near the eastern tower, however, recorded a sudden spike. Engineers could not decide whether this ______ pointed to real stress in the steel or simply to a faulty instrument.
questions.explanation: One reading that differs from all the others is an anomaly.

distractors.why: Consensus means general agreement, but this reading disagreed with the rest.
A paradox is a seeming contradiction; a single odd reading is just an irregularity.
A precedent is an earlier example that guides later decisions, which does not fit.

definition: to make pain or a problem less severe

examples.text: The new drug alleviates joint swelling without upsetting the stomach.
Relief programs were created to alleviate hunger during the long drought.
A short walk can alleviate the stress of studying for finals.

confused.note: Alleviate means to lessen a burden or pain; ameliorate means to make a bad situation better overall.

questions.passage: The clinic could not cure the disease, but its staff worked to ______ patients' discomfort, offering cool compresses, quiet rooms, and medicine to bring down their fevers.
questions.explanation: The staff could not cure but could lessen the discomfort.

distractors.why: Exacerbate means to make worse, the opposite of what caregivers intend.
Scrutinize means to examine closely; the listed actions soothe, they do not inspect.
Elicit means to draw out a response; the staff were reducing discomfort, not producing it.

definition: to support a statement or theory with evidence

examples.text: A second laboratory was able to corroborate the results using a different method.
Ship logs corroborate the sailor's account of the storm.
My sister corroborated my story that the dog, not I, had eaten the cake.

confused.note: Corroborate means to confirm with evidence; collaborate means to work together.

questions.passage: The diarist claimed that a comet had been visible over Paris for three nights in 1811. Astronomical records from an observatory in Vienna ______ her account, listing the same comet on the same dates.
questions.explanation: The independent records confirm what the diarist wrote.

distractors.why: Refute means to prove false, but the records match her account.
Collaborate means to work together; records cannot work with an account.
Embellish means to add decorative or invented details, which the records do not do.

definition: similar in a way that makes a comparison useful

examples.text: A bat's wing is analogous to a bird's wing, though the two evolved separately.
The council's role was analogous to that of a modern supreme court.
Learning chords on the ukulele is analogous to learning them on guitar, just with fewer strings.

confused.note: Analogous things are alike in some useful way; identical things are exactly the same.

questions.passage: To explain how a computer's memory works, the instructor described a wall of labeled mailboxes, each holding one slip of paper. The comparison was not perfect, but students found the mailboxes ______ enough to memory addresses to grasp the idea.
questions.explanation: The mailboxes are similar enough to make a helpful comparison.

distractors.why: Disparate means fundamentally different, which would make the comparison useless.
Arbitrary means chosen without reason; the comparison was chosen because it fits.
Superfluous means unnecessary, but the comparison helped students understand.

definition: very careful to be honest and to do things exactly right

examples.text: A scrupulous researcher, she reported even the results that weakened her own theory.
The clerk kept scrupulous records of every bushel of grain that entered the city.
Our treasurer is scrupulous about returning every cent of leftover club money.

confused.note: Both mean very careful; scrupulous adds a sense of moral care about doing what is right.

questions.passage: The accountant was known for being ______: she checked every figure twice and once returned a client's payment because he had overpaid by eleven cents.
questions.explanation: Double-checking and returning a tiny overpayment show careful honesty.

distractors.why: Negligent means careless, the opposite of checking every figure twice.
Erratic means unpredictable, but her behavior is consistent and exact.
Pragmatic means practical; refunding eleven cents shows exact honesty more than practicality.

definition: to reject something firmly or refuse to accept it

examples.text: The new government repudiated the debts run up by the former king.
After the data were exposed as faked, the journal repudiated the paper.
She repudiated the rumor that she planned to quit the team.

confused.note: To repudiate is to reject; to refute is to prove wrong with evidence.

questions.passage: Early in his career the architect praised glass towers as the future of cities. In later essays he came to ______ that view entirely, calling such buildings wasteful and cold.
questions.explanation: He firmly rejected the view he once held.

distractors.why: Corroborate means to confirm, but he turned against his earlier view.
Emulate means to imitate, which does not describe rejecting an opinion.
Mitigate means to make less severe; he did not soften the view, he rejected it.

definition: not regular or steady; unpredictable

examples.text: The comet followed an erratic path after passing close to Jupiter.
Supply shipments were so erratic that the fort often went weeks without flour.
Our old car's erratic engine might start on the first try or the tenth.

confused.note: Erratic means unpredictable and unsteady; eccentric means odd in a harmless, individual way.

questions.passage: The bus was supposed to arrive every fifteen minutes. In practice its schedule was ______: riders might wait five minutes one morning and forty the next, with no pattern anyone could detect.
questions.explanation: Wait times that vary with no pattern are unpredictable.

distractors.why: Meticulous means extremely careful and precise, the opposite of this schedule.
Stagnant means not moving or changing, but the wait times kept changing.
Ominous means threatening; the passage describes irregular timing, not a threat.

definition: to prove that a statement or theory is wrong

examples.text: The experiment refuted the idea that the bacteria needed sunlight to grow.
Newly found letters refute the legend that the two rivals never met.
I refuted my brother's claim that I never do dishes by showing him the chore chart.

confused.note: To refute is to prove wrong; to repudiate is simply to reject.

questions.passage: For years, textbooks stated that the island's first settlers arrived around the year 1200. Charcoal from ancient cooking fires, dated to roughly 800, appears to ______ that claim.
questions.explanation: Evidence four centuries older proves the textbook date wrong.

distractors.why: Corroborate means to confirm, but the charcoal conflicts with the claim.
Repudiate means to reject or disown, something a person does; evidence disproves a claim.
Exacerbate means to worsen a problem, which does not apply to a claim.

definition: to make something less harmful, serious, or painful

examples.text: Planting trees along the river helps mitigate erosion during spring floods.
Rationing was introduced to mitigate the effects of the wartime shortage.
Wearing a helmet will not prevent a fall, but it can mitigate the injury.

confused.note: Mitigate means to lessen; militate (usually "militate against") means to work as a force against something.

questions.passage: No seawall can stop a hurricane outright. Still, coastal engineers argue that restored marshes can ______ a storm's damage by absorbing much of the force of the waves before they reach homes.
questions.explanation: The marshes cannot stop the storm, but they can reduce the harm.

distractors.why: Exacerbate means to make worse, the opposite of absorbing waves.
Preclude means to prevent entirely, but the passage says the storm cannot be stopped.
Vindicate means to clear of blame, which does not apply to storm damage.

definition: careful to think about all risks before acting or speaking

examples.text: The ambassador was circumspect, never committing his country to a promise in writing.
The heroine gives circumspect answers until she learns whom she can trust.
Be circumspect about what you post online, since future employers may read it.

confused.note: Circumspect is an adjective meaning cautious; circumvent is a verb meaning to get around something.

questions.passage: Asked by reporters whether the merger would lead to layoffs, the usually talkative executive grew ______, saying only that "all options are being reviewed" and declining to offer details.
questions.explanation: Giving a guarded answer and no details shows caution.

distractors.why: Candid means open and direct, but the executive avoided specifics.
Belligerent means hostile and ready to fight; the executive was guarded, not aggressive.
Eloquent means fluent and persuasive, yet the executive said very little.

definition: a statement or situation that seems to contradict itself but may still be true

examples.text: It is a paradox of deserts that flash floods are among their greatest dangers.
The play turns on a paradox: the king must lose his crown to become a true ruler.
It is a paradox that the more options a menu has, the harder it is to feel happy with my order.

confused.note: A paradox seems self-contradictory yet may be true; irony is a gap between what is expected and what happens or is meant.

questions.passage: Economists have noted a ______ in how people save: workers who are given more retirement plans to choose from are actually less likely to enroll in any of them.
questions.explanation: More choice leading to less action seems contradictory but is true.

distractors.why: Consensus means general agreement, which does not describe a surprising pattern.
A precedent is an earlier example used as a guide, not a seeming contradiction.
A nuance is a subtle distinction; the passage describes an outright seeming contradiction.

definition: based on observation or experiment, not on theory alone

examples.text: The model looked elegant, but it needed empirical testing in real rivers.
Galileo favored empirical evidence over the authority of ancient texts.
My empirical research, meaning tasting six brands, shows the cheapest salsa is the best.

confused.note: Empirical claims rest on data from observation; theoretical claims rest on reasoning and models.

questions.passage: The belief that plants grow faster when spoken to had circulated for decades as folk wisdom. Dr. Okafor wanted ______ support for it, so she measured the growth of two hundred seedlings under controlled conditions.
questions.explanation: She gathered measured data, which is evidence from observation.

distractors.why: Anecdotal evidence comes from personal stories, the kind of support she wanted to move beyond.
Rhetorical relates to persuasive language, not to measured data.
Nominal means in name only or very small, which does not describe evidence from experiments.

definition: to give evidence that shows a claim is true

examples.text: The team could not substantiate its claim without samples from a second site.
No surviving document substantiates the story that the queen visited the village.
If you say the store overcharged you, bring the receipt to substantiate it.

confused.note: Substantiate is a verb meaning to prove; substantial is an adjective meaning large or solid.

questions.passage: The biographer asserts that the composer wrote her final symphony in a single week. Yet he offers no letters, drafts, or diary entries to ______ this assertion, and readers are left to take it on faith.
questions.explanation: Letters and drafts would be evidence to support the assertion.

distractors.why: Refute means to disprove; the biographer would want to support his own claim.
Disseminate means to spread widely, which is not what evidence does for a claim.
Lament means to express sorrow, which does not fit offering evidence.

definition: clear, logical, and convincing

examples.text: Her cogent speech persuaded the assembly to fund the canal.
The paper makes a cogent case that the fossils belong to a single species.
My sister gave such a cogent argument for a later curfew that our parents agreed.

confused.note: Coherent means logically connected and easy to follow; cogent adds that the argument is convincing.

questions.passage: The committee had expected to reject the proposal. But the student's presentation was so ______, moving step by step from the data to a well-supported recommendation, that every member voted in favor.
questions.explanation: A step-by-step, well-supported case that wins every vote is clear and convincing.

distractors.why: Tenuous means weak or flimsy, which would not win unanimous support.
Verbose means wordy; the passage praises the logic, not the length.
Dogmatic means stubbornly opinionated, but the case was built on data.

definition: to make something clear by explaining it

examples.text: The diagram elucidates how the heart's four chambers work together.
The editor's footnotes elucidate references that modern readers would miss.
Could you elucidate the rules of cricket for those of us who have never watched it?

confused.note: Elucidate means to explain; elicit means to draw out a response.

questions.passage: The physics lecture left many students confused about how waves can cancel each other. In the next class, the professor used two overlapping ripples in a tank of water to ______ the concept.
questions.explanation: The demonstration was meant to make a confusing idea clear.

distractors.why: Obscure as a verb means to make unclear, the opposite of the professor's aim.
Elicit means to draw out a reaction; a concept is explained, not drawn out.
Repudiate means to reject, but the professor was teaching the concept.

partsNote: to bring out into the light

definition: happening by chance, especially in a lucky way

examples.text: The discovery of penicillin began with a fortuitous spot of mold on a lab dish.
A fortuitous shift in the wind saved the fleet from the rocks.
It was fortuitous that I ran into my teacher just when I needed a recommendation letter.

confused.note: Fortunate means lucky; fortuitous stresses that something happened by chance, and it is usually a happy chance.

questions.passage: The two researchers had never planned to work together. Their partnership began with a ______ meeting: both happened to be stranded in the same airport during a snowstorm and started comparing notes.
questions.explanation: Being stranded in the same airport was a lucky accident.

distractors.why: Deliberate means planned on purpose, but the meeting was unplanned.
Ominous suggests something bad is coming, yet the meeting led to a good partnership.
Perfunctory means done with little effort or interest, which does not describe a chance meeting.

definition: to make a bad situation better

examples.text: Reformers pushed for laws to ameliorate conditions in crowded factory housing.
Adding compost can ameliorate poor soil within a single growing season.
A fan and an open window did little to ameliorate the heat in the attic bedroom.

confused.note: Ameliorate means to improve a bad situation; alleviate means to lessen pain or a burden.

questions.passage: The village's only well often ran dry by midsummer. To ______ the shortage, engineers built stone channels that carried snowmelt down from the hills, and within two years families no longer had to ration water.
questions.explanation: The channels improved a bad situation, ending the need to ration.

distractors.why: Exacerbate means to make worse, the opposite of what the channels did.
Disparage means to speak of with disrespect, which does not fit fixing a shortage.
Scrutinize means to examine closely; the engineers acted to fix the shortage, not just study it.

definition: insisting that one's beliefs are right and refusing to consider other views

examples.text: The council's dogmatic leaders banned any book that questioned their teachings.
A good scientist avoids being dogmatic and stays willing to revise a theory.
My uncle is so dogmatic about grilling that he will not even try a gas barbecue.

confused.note: Dogmatic means bound to fixed beliefs; pragmatic means guided by what works.

questions.passage: Professor Hale welcomed questions but rarely changed his mind. Colleagues described him as ______: when new excavations challenged his theory about the city's founding, he dismissed the findings without reading the full report.
questions.explanation: Dismissing evidence unread shows a rigid refusal to reconsider a belief.

distractors.why: Pragmatic means practical and adaptable, the opposite of ignoring new evidence.
Diffident means shy and lacking confidence, but he was overly sure of himself.
Meticulous means careful about details, yet he did not even read the report.

definition: relating to beauty or to how something looks

examples.text: The poet cared more about aesthetic effect than about telling a clear story.
The bridge's curved cables serve a structural purpose as well as an aesthetic one.
We chose the blue tiles for purely aesthetic reasons, since both kinds cost the same.

confused.note: Aesthetic relates to beauty; ascetic describes a person who lives with strict self-denial.

questions.passage: The engineers insisted that the new lampposts needed only to be bright and cheap. The city's design board disagreed, arguing that ______ concerns mattered too, since residents would have to look at the posts every day.
questions.explanation: Concerns about how the posts look are concerns about appearance and beauty.

distractors.why: Utilitarian means focused on usefulness, which is the engineers' view, not the board's added concern.
Ascetic describes strict self-denial, a look-alike word that has nothing to do with appearance.
Empirical means based on observation or data, which is not the board's point.

definition: more important than anything else

examples.text: For the besieged city, securing a supply of fresh water was paramount.
In vaccine trials, the safety of volunteers is the paramount concern.
Getting enough sleep before the exam is paramount, so close the laptop by ten.

confused.note: Paramount means most important; tantamount means equal in effect to something.

questions.passage: The expedition's leader reminded the climbers that reaching the summit was only a secondary goal. The safety of the team was ______, and she would order a retreat at the first sign of a storm.
questions.explanation: Safety outranks the secondary goal, so it is the most important concern.

distractors.why: Peripheral means of minor importance, the opposite of what the leader stresses.
Tantamount means equivalent to something else and needs "to"; it does not mean most important.
Arbitrary means based on whim, which does not describe a firm priority.

definition: kind and wishing to do good for others

examples.text: The benevolent merchant paid for a school that the town's poorest children could attend.
The tale's benevolent giant guards the valley and asks for nothing in return.
A benevolent neighbor shoveled our driveway before we even woke up.

confused.note: Benevolent means wishing good to others; malevolent means wishing them harm.

questions.passage: Townspeople had assumed that the factory owner cared only about profit. They revised that opinion after her ______ decision to keep paying workers' full wages during the three months the plant was closed for repairs.
questions.explanation: Paying wages while the plant was closed is a kind, generous act.

distractors.why: Malevolent means wishing harm, the opposite of this generosity.
Frugal means careful about spending, but she chose the costly option.
Arbitrary means random or without reason; the decision is presented as kind, not random.

definition: to express deep sadness or regret about something

examples.text: In the poem, a sailor laments the loss of his ship and crew.
Editorials lamented the closing of the last streetcar line in 1954.
My grandmother often laments that nobody writes letters by hand anymore.

confused.note: Lament means to grieve over something; lambaste means to criticize harshly.

questions.passage: Longtime residents ______ the loss of the old theater, recalling the first films they saw there and wishing aloud that the city had found the money to save it.
questions.explanation: Recalling fond memories and wishing it had been saved express sorrow and regret.

distractors.why: Extol means to praise highly; the residents are grieving a loss, not praising it.
Condone means to accept or overlook wrongdoing, which does not fit grieving a loss.
Vindicate means to clear of blame, which has nothing to do with sorrow.

definition: extremely careful about small details

examples.text: Her meticulous notes let other chemists repeat the experiment exactly.
The mapmaker's meticulous survey marked every well and footpath in the valley.
My brother is meticulous about his sneakers and cleans them after every wear.

confused.note: Meticulous means careful about details; fastidious means hard to please and fussy about standards.

questions.passage: Everyone at the museum agreed that the restorer's work was ______: before touching the painting, she photographed every square inch, tested each pigment, and recorded the direction of each brushstroke.
questions.explanation: Photographing, testing, and recording everything shows extreme attention to detail.

distractors.why: Cursory means quick and superficial, the opposite of this thorough preparation.
Erratic means inconsistent and unpredictable, but her process was orderly.
Ostentatious means showy; her careful work is not described as showing off.

definition: able to express ideas clearly and movingly in speech or writing

examples.text: Douglass was an eloquent speaker whose lectures drew crowds across the North.
The novel's most eloquent passage describes rain falling on an empty farm.
Her eloquent toast at the wedding had half the guests in tears.

confused.note: Eloquent means speaking well; loquacious means speaking a great deal.

questions.passage: Few expected the shy, soft-spoken chemist to hold an audience's attention. Yet her acceptance speech proved so ______, weaving her research into the story of her grandmother's garden, that listeners rose to applaud.
questions.explanation: A moving, well-crafted speech that earns an ovation is expressive and persuasive.

distractors.why: Reticent means unwilling to speak, which the speech disproved.
Verbose means using too many words, a criticism that does not fit a speech that moved its audience.
Pedantic means showing off minor learning in a dull way, the wrong tone for a moving speech.

definition: to spread information or ideas widely

examples.text: The printing press made it possible to disseminate pamphlets across Europe in weeks.
Health agencies disseminate flu guidance through schools and clinics.
The club uses a group chat to disseminate news about schedule changes.

confused.note: Disseminate means to spread widely; dissipate means to fade away or scatter until gone.

questions.passage: In the 1840s, a new scientific finding might take months to reach readers overseas. The telegraph changed that, allowing newspapers to ______ reports of discoveries to distant cities within hours.
questions.explanation: Sending reports to distant cities is spreading information widely.

distractors.why: Suppress means to hold back, the opposite of what the telegraph made possible.
Dissipate means to scatter and disappear; the reports were spread, not lost.
Fabricate means to invent falsely, which the passage does not suggest.

partsNote: from Latin semen, "seed": to scatter seeds

definition: to speak about someone or something as having little worth

examples.text: The critic disparaged the novel as "a long walk to nowhere."
Rival newspapers disparaged the inventor until his lamp lit an entire street.
Do not disparage your teammate's idea before you have heard all of it.

confused.note: Disparage is a verb meaning to belittle; disparate is an adjective meaning very different.

questions.passage: Although the two chefs had trained together, they were hardly friends. In interviews each would ______ the other's cooking, one calling his rival's sauces "wallpaper paste" and the other dismissing her dishes as "expensive snacks."
questions.explanation: The insulting quotations show each chef belittling the other's work.

distractors.why: Emulate means to imitate out of admiration, the opposite of these insults.
Corroborate means to confirm with evidence, which does not describe insults.
Placate means to calm someone's anger; insults would do the reverse.

partsNote: from Old French for "lower in rank"

definition: to show that someone or something was right or not guilty after doubt

examples.text: Later evidence vindicated the captain, who had been blamed for the wreck.
The discovery of the particle vindicated a theory proposed forty years earlier.
The security video vindicated my claim that I had locked the gym door.

confused.note: Vindicate means to clear from blame; vindictive means eager for revenge.

questions.passage: When Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents drift, most geologists mocked the idea. Decades later, mapping of the seafloor revealed spreading ridges that could push continents apart, and his theory was at last ______.
questions.explanation: The seafloor evidence showed that his ridiculed theory had been right.

distractors.why: Refuted means proved wrong, but the evidence supported him.
Relegated means pushed to a lower position; the theory gained standing.
Lamented means mourned, which does not fit a theory being proved right.

partsNote: from Latin vindicare, "to claim, to set free"

definition: done secretly, especially because it would not be approved of

examples.text: The spy takes a surreptitious photograph of the map while the general pours tea.
Surreptitious meetings in a cellar kept the banned newspaper alive.
He stole a surreptitious glance at his phone during the lecture.

confused.note: Both mean secret; surreptitious stresses quick, sneaky action, while clandestine stresses planned secrecy.

questions.passage: Museum rules forbade any contact with the sculptures. Still, a guard noticed one visitor reach out for a ______ touch of the marble when he thought nobody was looking.
questions.explanation: A forbidden touch made when nobody seems to be looking is sneaky and secret.

distractors.why: Overt means done openly, but the visitor acted when he thought he was unobserved.
Benevolent means kind, which has nothing to do with sneaking a touch.
Perfunctory means done without care or interest; the stress here is on secrecy.

definition: general agreement among the members of a group

examples.text: There is a strong consensus among climate scientists that the planet is warming.
The delegates argued for weeks before reaching a consensus on the new flag.
After an hour of debate, the consensus was pizza.

confused.note: Consensus means general agreement; a census is an official count of a population.

questions.passage: For much of the last century, nutrition researchers disagreed sharply about how much salt is safe. In recent years, however, something close to a ______ has emerged, with most major health organizations now recommending similar limits.
questions.explanation: Most organizations now recommending similar limits shows general agreement.

distractors.why: A paradox is a seeming contradiction, not agreement among experts.
A discrepancy is a difference between things that should match, the opposite of agreement.
An anomaly is something that departs from the norm, not a shared view.

definition: very skilled at something

examples.text: Adept at languages, the young envoy could bargain in four tongues.
Octopuses are adept at squeezing through gaps barely wider than their eyes.
My cousin is so adept at parallel parking that she does it in one move.

confused.note: Adept means skilled; adapt means to change to fit new conditions. Adopt means to take as one's own.

questions.passage: Nothing in Rivera's first clumsy attempts suggested a gift for glassblowing. After two years of daily practice, though, she had become remarkably ______, shaping delicate stems that her teacher admitted he could not match.
questions.explanation: Work her teacher cannot match shows she became highly skilled.

distractors.why: Inept means unskilled, which describes only her first attempts.
Complacent means smugly satisfied, but she practiced daily to improve.
Diffident means lacking confidence, which is not what the passage describes.

definition: clear and easy to understand

examples.text: Her lucid explanation of black holes made sense even to the youngest visitors.
The essayist's lucid prose never forces a reader to reread a sentence.
The manual was so lucid that I set up the printer in five minutes.

confused.note: Lucid means clear; lurid means shockingly vivid or sensational.

questions.passage: Tax law is famously hard to follow, so reviewers were delighted by the new guide. Its author manages to be ______ throughout, defining each term in plain words and walking readers through one worked example at a time.
questions.explanation: Plain definitions and step-by-step examples make the guide clear.

distractors.why: Convoluted means complicated and hard to follow, the opposite of this guide.
Esoteric means understood only by a few experts, but the guide is written for general readers.
Terse means brief to the point of seeming curt; the guide takes time to explain.

definition: extremely and obviously bad

examples.text: The court called the forged land deeds an egregious abuse of public trust.
Leaving out half the data was an egregious error that sank the study.
The referee missed an egregious foul that everyone in the gym could see.

confused.note: Egregious means shockingly bad; gregarious means sociable.

questions.passage: Small rounding mistakes are common in budget reports and are usually forgiven. The auditor's letter, however, described an error of a different order: an ______ miscalculation that overstated the town's income by forty million dollars.
questions.explanation: A forty-million-dollar overstatement is glaringly and seriously wrong.

distractors.why: Negligible means too small to matter, which fits the rounding mistakes, not this error.
Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning; the error is clear and large.
Inadvertent means accidental; the sentence contrasts size and seriousness, not intent.

definition: to prevent something from happening or make it impossible

examples.text: The thick cloud cover precluded any view of the eclipse.
The treaty precluded either nation from building forts along the border.
A sprained ankle precluded her from running in Saturday's race.

confused.note: Preclude means to make something impossible in advance; exclude means to leave someone or something out.

questions.passage: The grant's rules do not ______ applicants from seeking additional funding elsewhere; in fact, the foundation encourages scholars to combine its awards with support from other sources.
questions.explanation: "In fact, the foundation encourages" shows the rules do not prevent other funding.

distractors.why: Exempt means to free from a duty, which does not fit "from seeking additional funding."
Compel means to force; "do not compel applicants from seeking" is neither logical nor grammatical.
Elicit means to draw out a response, which does not fit rules and applicants.

definition: lasting for a very short time

examples.text: Desert wildflowers are ephemeral, blooming for only a few days after rain.
The poem compares youth to the ephemeral glow of a firefly.
Internet fame can be ephemeral; last month's viral star is already forgotten.

confused.note: Ephemeral means short-lived; ethereal means delicate and light, as if not of this world.

questions.passage: Ice sculptors accept that their art is ______. A carving that takes three days to complete may begin to drip within hours, and by the end of the festival nothing remains but a puddle.
questions.explanation: Work that melts within hours or days is short-lived.

distractors.why: Enduring means lasting, the opposite of a sculpture that melts.
Meticulous means very careful; the sentences that follow are about how briefly the art lasts.
Austere means severely plain, which the passage does not discuss.

definition: spreading through every part of something

examples.text: The scent of sulfur is pervasive near the hot springs.
Fear of spies was pervasive in the capital during the war.
The smell of burnt popcorn was pervasive on the whole third floor.

confused.note: Pervasive means spread throughout; persuasive means able to convince.

questions.passage: The researchers expected to find the invasive vine only along the riverbank. Instead it proved ______, appearing in every one of the forty forest plots they surveyed, including those on dry ridges far from water.
questions.explanation: Turning up in all forty plots means the vine had spread throughout the forest.

distractors.why: Ephemeral means short-lived, but the passage concerns how widely the vine spread.
Benign means harmless, which says nothing about how widespread the vine is.
Sporadic means occurring only here and there, but the vine was in every plot.

definition: lasting only a short time; staying briefly

examples.text: The drug caused transient dizziness that passed within an hour.
The mining camp had a transient population that vanished when the silver ran out.
The joy of a new phone is transient; in a month it is just a phone.

confused.note: Transient means short-lived or passing through; transit is movement from one place to another.

questions.passage: Doctors reassured the patient that the numbness in her hand was ______. Such symptoms, they explained, usually fade on their own within a day or two and leave no lasting damage.
questions.explanation: Symptoms that fade within a day or two are temporary.

distractors.why: Chronic means lasting a long time or recurring, the opposite of fading in a day.
Egregious means shockingly bad, which would not reassure a patient.
Latent means present but hidden; her numbness was noticeable, just brief.

definition: a strong feeling of dislike

examples.text: The narrator's antipathy toward his stepfather colors every scene they share.
Mutual antipathy between the two generals nearly cost the army the campaign.
I have a lifelong antipathy to cilantro, which tastes like soap to me.

confused.note: Antipathy is strong dislike; apathy is a lack of any feeling or interest.

questions.passage: The two composers rarely spoke, and their ______ was well known. Each refused to attend the other's premieres, and one reportedly crossed the street to avoid meeting his rival.
questions.explanation: Refusing to attend premieres and avoiding each other show strong dislike.

distractors.why: Apathy is a lack of feeling; crossing the street to avoid someone shows strong feeling.
Affinity means natural liking, the opposite of their relationship.
Deference means respectful yielding, which neither composer showed.

definition: to move someone or something to a lower or less important position

examples.text: After the coup, the old ministers were relegated to posts in distant provinces.
The editor relegated the poet's best lines to a footnote.
My old bike has been relegated to the back of the garage since I got the new one.

confused.note: Relegate means to push down to a lesser place; delegate means to hand a task to someone else.

questions.passage: Early histories of computing celebrated a handful of famous engineers. The women who wrote the first programs were often ______ to a brief mention, if they appeared at all.
questions.explanation: Being reduced to a brief mention means being pushed to a minor place.

distractors.why: Elevated means raised in importance, the opposite of a brief mention.
Delegated means assigned a task to someone; it does not mean reduced in importance.
Vindicated means proved right, which a brief mention does not accomplish.

definition: the feeling that someone or something is not worthy of respect

examples.text: The duchess looks at the muddy travelers with open disdain.
The court painter's disdain for street artists kept them out of the academy.
My cat regards the new, expensive bed with disdain and sleeps in the box it came in.

confused.note: Disdain is the standard word for contempt; "distain" is an old word for staining and is almost never correct.

questions.passage: The veteran reporters made no effort to hide their ______ for the new social media team, rolling their eyes in meetings and referring to its videos as "cartoons for adults."
questions.explanation: Eye-rolling and mocking nicknames show a lack of respect.

distractors.why: Deference means respectful submission, the opposite of mockery.
Empathy means sharing another's feelings, which the reporters do not show.
Nostalgia is fond longing for the past, which does not describe mockery.

partsNote: from Latin dignus, "worthy": to treat as unworthy

definition: to support or strengthen

examples.text: Three new fossils bolster the theory that the species walked upright.
The alliance bolstered the small kingdom's defenses against invasion.
A good breakfast bolstered my confidence before the driving test.

confused.note: Both mean to help; bolster stresses propping up something that needs support, while boost stresses lifting it higher.

questions.passage: The claim that the mural dates to the 1300s once rested on a single document. A recent chemical analysis of its pigments, which matches paints used in that century, has ______ the claim considerably.
questions.explanation: New matching evidence adds support to a claim that once had little.

distractors.why: Undermined means weakened, but the analysis agrees with the claim.
Disseminated means spread widely; the analysis supports the claim, it does not publicize it.
Precluded means prevented, which does not fit new evidence that agrees with the claim.

definition: based on chance or personal whim instead of reason or a system

examples.text: The governor's arbitrary arrests turned the merchants against him.
The cutoff of 100 samples was arbitrary; nothing in the method required that number.
The seating chart felt arbitrary, as if the teacher had drawn names from a hat.

confused.note: Arbitrary means without reason or system; arbitrate means to settle a dispute as a neutral judge.

questions.passage: Critics of the scholarship complained that its age limit seemed ______. Why, they asked, should a student who turned twenty-five in June qualify while one who turned twenty-five in May did not, when nothing about their records differed?
questions.explanation: A cutoff that separates identical students for no stated reason seems based on whim.

distractors.why: Judicious means showing good judgment, the opposite of the critics' complaint.
Lenient means not strict, but the critics object to the lack of reason, not to mildness.
Ambiguous means unclear in meaning; the rule is clear, just not justified.
